The most important conceptual shift is the reactivity engine. Vue 2's

approach had to walk every property of an object up front and define getters/setters for each one — which is why adding a brand-new property to a reactive object in Vue 2 silently didn't work unless you used
operations on an object (get, set, delete, has, and array methods) without needing to know the property names in advance, which is why this restriction disappears in Vue 3.
Composition API vs Options API — Which Should You Learn?
Composition API as the primary style
because it's what the Vue team recommends for new projects and what you'll see in modern codebases, third-party libraries, and the official documentation's default examples. But you will see the

constantly — in Vue 2 migrations, in older tutorials, and in codebases where teams simply prefer its structure. Every chapter that introduces a new concept will show both styles side by side so you can read either fluently, even though your own code should default to Composition API with
Here's the same tiny counter component in both styles, to set the pattern you'll see repeated throughout this course:

<script>
export default {
  data() {
    return { count: 0 }
  },
  computed: {
    doubled() {
      return this.count * 2
    }
  },
  methods: {
    increment() {
      this.count++
    }
  }
}
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="increment">
    Count: {{ count }} (doubled: {{ doubled }})
  </button>
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const doubled = computed(() => count.value * 2)

function increment() {
  count.value++
}
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="increment">
    Count: {{ count }} (doubled: {{ doubled }})
  </button>
</template>
Both render identically. The Options API groups code by
(all data together, all methods together); the Composition API groups code by

A developer ports this Options API component from a Vue 2 tutorial and reports that every card on the page shares the same "expanded" state — clicking one expands all of them.
is declared once, at module scope, outside the component definition. Every instance of
in one instance mutates the one shared object that every other instance also reads from. This has nothing to do with Vue 2 vs Vue 3 — it's a plain JavaScript reference-sharing bug that
being a function is specifically designed to prevent, as long as the object it returns is created fresh inside the function.
The fix is to construct the object inside
so each component instance gets its own independent copy:

<script>
export default {
  data() {
    return { expanded: false }
  },
  methods: {
    toggle() {
      this.expanded = !this.expanded
    }
  }
}
</script>
being a function isn't a stylistic preference — it's what guarantees every component instance gets a fresh, independent state object instead of sharing one by closure or module-level reference.
